reason: The chapter’s top-ranked candidate, on a five-word run that the verse then repeats twice more. 1 Kings 21:15-16 is Ahab going down to take possession of Naboth’s vineyard after Jezebel has had Naboth stoned, and the surface attraction is real: in both texts a party seizes land whose owners are gone. But the transaction is inverted at the point that matters. Naboth’s vineyard is seized from a man judicially murdered for it, and the seizure is the crime the chapter exists to condemn; the robbers take lands the Nephites have deliberately abandoned under Lachoneus’s proclamation (3 Nephi 3:13, 3:22), which is why the lands are empty and why, four verses later, the robbers are starving in them. Ahab gets a vineyard; Giddianhi gets a desert. Nothing of 1 Kings 21 beyond the idiom is present, and “take possession of” is the ordinary King James phrase for occupying land.

sharedText: their flocks, and their herds, and all their substance
reason: A genuine composite of two Genesis migrations sits under this clause — “and all their substance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 12:5, where Abram leaves Haran for Canaan with it, and “flocks and their herds and all” occurs in exactly two, Genesis 46:32 and 47:1, where Jacob’s household goes down into Egypt. But 3 Nephi 4:3 is not where the Book of Mormon says it. The phrase enters at 3 Nephi 3:13, in Lachoneus’s proclamation commanding the gathering (“their flocks and their herds, and all their substance, save it were their land, unto one place”), and is executed at 3:22. 4:3 is the narrator recalling a movement already narrated. Adjudicate the Genesis composite at 3 Nephi 3:13; this row exists so that a reader who meets the phrase here is sent there.

A five-word run, and the highest-scoring candidate on the verse, on a phrase the catalogue has good reason to take seriously: John 18:14 is Caiaphas’s counsel that it was expedient that one man should die for the people, and 1 Nephi 4:13 borrows precisely that sentence to justify the killing of Laban. So the temptation here is not naive. It fails on sense. Caiaphas’s expediency is a calculation that one death will save a nation, and the Gospel glosses it as unwitting prophecy; Giddianhi’s is a supply problem — “there was no way that they could subsist, save it were to plunder, and rob, and murder”. Nothing dies for anyone, nobody prophesies, and “expedient” is among the most worn words in the Book of Mormon’s vocabulary, appearing across every book with no biblical colouring at all. The Caiaphas link stands at 1 Nephi 4:13 and does not extend here.

This is the closer verbal match of the two and it still loses. “fallen to the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 26:14 and 2 Chronicles 20:24, and Acts has the Book of Mormon’s “all” as well — “when we were all fallen to the earth”, against “had all fallen to the earth”. What Acts does not have is anything else. Paul is recounting his own conversion on the Damascus road, struck down by a light while travelling to arrest Christians, and hears a voice; the Nephite armies fall down deliberately, in prayer, at the sight of an approaching enemy. 2 Chronicles 20:24, by contrast, sits inside the one KJV narrative whose entire sequence 3 Nephi 4 reproduces — the gathering, the prostration, the ambush the Lord sets, the field of dead, the return with singing. The link is written there; see the note at 4:8 for the argument, including the admission that Chronicles supplies the pattern and Acts the extra word.

“threatenings” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 4:29 and Acts 9:1, and in no Old Testament verse — a genuine New-Testament-only word turning up in a first-century-BC Nephite war narrative, which is the kind of datum this catalogue exists for. It is not adjudicated here for two reasons. First, the word enters this book at 3 Nephi 3:12, of Lachoneus refusing to be frightened by “the demands and the threatenings of a robber”, so 4:12 is a repetition inside one book (ADJUDICATING §4). Second, and decisively, the full Acts 9:1 collocation appears one chapter later: 3 Nephi 5:5 reads “as many as were found breathing out threatenings against their brethren”, against Acts 9:1’s “Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord”. That is where the borrowing is demonstrable and that is where it should be catalogued. Noted here so a reader of 4:12 is sent to 5:5.

A five-word run of pure geographical connective. Joshua 13:4 is a boundary list — “all the land of the Canaanites… unto Aphek, to the borders of the Amorites” — and 3 Nephi 4:13 is a pursuit order bounded by the wilderness. No content word is shared beyond the idiom itself, and the Book of Mormon uses “the borders of” for every frontier it has. This entry covers the other boundary-formula candidates in the chapter; they are not listed individually.

“with boldness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 4:31, where the disciples filled with the Holy Ghost “spake the word of God with boldness” — and the temptation is sharpened by the fact that Acts 4:29, two verses earlier, is one of the King James Bible’s only two “threatenings” verses, and 3 Nephi 4:12 has “threatenings”. Two words from one short Acts paragraph, two verses apart in the Book of Mormon, is a coincidence worth stating. It is not enough. In Acts the threatenings belong to the persecutors and the boldness to the persecuted, and both words are about speech; in 3 Nephi 4 both belong to Giddianhi, and the boldness is a robber chief’s courage in a losing fight. Boldness is also among the Book of Mormon’s most common virtues, and it is never Acts’s. Recorded so that the convergence is on the books, and declined.

“lay siege” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Isaiah 29:3 and Ezekiel 4:2-3, so Ezekiel is a real candidate on the phrase alone. Isaiah 29:3 takes it because it is the only one of the three that has the Book of Mormon’s “round about” attached — “I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount”, against “they came up on all sides to lay siege round about the people of Nephi”. Ezekiel 4:2 is a symbolic action performed on a tile with a model fort and battering rams, and none of its furniture is present. The link is written at 4:16 with Isaiah 29:3 in composite alongside Luke 19:43.

A five-word run consisting entirely of function words plus “people”. 1 Chronicles 23:25 is David’s reason for settling the Levites’ duties, “The LORD God of Israel hath given rest unto his people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever”; 3 Nephi 4:23 is Zemnarihah ordering a retreat northward. Opposed in sense — rest granted against a siege abandoned — and sharing no distinctive vocabulary. Covered in principle by the standing connective-tissue exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

sharedText: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob
reason: The obvious source for the patriarchal triad, and the one the Book of Mormon does not use. Exodus 3:6, 3:15 and 4:5 all read “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”, with no conjunction before Isaac; 3:16 compresses to “of Isaac, and of Jacob”. 3 Nephi 4:30 has the conjunction, which puts it with Matthew 22:32, Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37 and Acts 7:32 — the four New Testament verses that are the only KJV verses reading it that way. Registered here because a reader who assumes Exodus should be told that the wording rules it out, and because tools/mediation-check.py cannot make the call: it ignores single common words, and “and” is the only word at which the two forms differ. Same discrimination as 1 Nephi 6:4 and Alma 36:2.

“most high God” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses, spread from Melchizedek in Genesis 14 to Daniel to the Gerasene demoniac in Mark 5:7, and no one of them can be picked out as a source. Psalm 78:56 ranked only because it is the shortest verse containing the phrase. It is also the wrong sense: “Yet they tempted and provoked the most high God, and kept not his testimonies” is about apostasy, and 3 Nephi 4:32 is a doxology. The title is doing real work in the verse — see the link at 4:32, where it answers Matthew 21:9’s “Hosanna in the highest” — but it is doing it as generic KJV vocabulary, not as a citation of any verse that has it.

The machine’s top candidate at 4:8, 4:31 and 4:33 alike, on a six-word run, and it is exactly backwards. Judges 2:14 is a judgment: “the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of spoilers… and he sold them into the hands of their enemies round about.” Every occurrence in 3 Nephi 4 is a deliverance OUT of those hands — 4:8 petitions it, 4:31 and 4:33 celebrate it. Judges 8:34, which has the Book of Mormon’s direction and its plural “hands”, is the verse the link is written on at 4:33; “delivered them out of the hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and that is it. This entry covers the Judges 2:14 candidate wherever it recurs in the chapter.
